questions.q: Why do residual connections (`x = x + sublayer(x)`) help when training very deep stacks of transformer blocks?
options: They reduce the total number of parameters in the model
They give the gradient a direct identity path backward through every block, alongside the path through the sublayer's weights
They remove the need for an activation function in the feed-forward sublayer
They make the model's output shape smaller
questions.explain: The '+' creates an identity shortcut that gradients can always flow through during backpropagation, preventing vanishing gradients across many stacked blocks — conceptually similar to an LSTM's additive cell-state path.

questions.q: Over which dimension does `nn.LayerNorm(d_model)` compute its mean and variance?
options: Across the batch dimension, for each position
Across the sequence length dimension, for each feature
Across the d_model feature dimension, independently for each token
Across both batch and sequence simultaneously
questions.explain: LayerNorm normalizes each token independently, computing mean and variance over that token's own d_model features — not across the batch or the sequence.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between post-norm (`norm(x + sublayer(x))`) and pre-norm (`x + sublayer(norm(x))`)?
options: Post-norm uses more parameters than pre-norm
Pre-norm removes the residual connection entirely
In pre-norm, the residual (identity) path is never touched by normalization; in post-norm, it is normalized at every block
They are mathematically identical and differ only in variable names
questions.explain: Pre-norm normalizes only the branch feeding into the sublayer, leaving `x` on the residual side completely clean. Post-norm normalizes the sum, which means the identity path gets rescaled every block.

questions.q: What is the main practical advantage of pre-norm over post-norm for modern large language models?
options: Pre-norm always achieves better final accuracy at every model size
Pre-norm requires fewer training examples
Pre-norm gives much more stable gradients, making it far easier to train deep stacks without careful learning-rate warmup
Pre-norm eliminates the need for a feed-forward sublayer
questions.explain: Keeping the residual path free of normalization gives pre-norm models dramatically more stable gradients, which is why GPT-2 and most modern LLMs use it despite post-norm sometimes edging it out at small scale.

questions.q: Which placement does this course's `TransformerBlock` (Lesson 37) and `TinyGPT` (Lesson 40) use?
options: Post-norm, matching the original 2017 paper exactly
Pre-norm, normalizing inside each branch before the sublayer runs
No normalization at all
A mix: post-norm for attention, pre-norm for the feed-forward sublayer
questions.explain: Both are written as `x = x + attn(norm1(x))` and `x = x + ffn(norm2(x))` — normalization happens before each sublayer, which is the pre-norm ordering.
